newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan election in sight, but issues out of focus.
newsitem.headline: Japan election in sight, but issues out of focus.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto this week gave the clearest sign yet that he will soon call elections to allow Japan's voters to pass judgment on a right-left coalition formed in 1994 without their input.

Hashimoto, Japan's fourth prime minister since it last voted in 1993, told a crowd of supporters: "In the not-so-distant future, the day of judgment for the Lower House will come under the new electoral system."
Hashimoto's speech to Liberal Democratic Party faithful appeared to confirm feverish media speculation that he would call snap polls next month.
But, like his counterparts across the non-communist political spectrum, LDP president Hashimoto was not clear about what it is voters will be asked to judge.

No single party is expected to capture a simple majority in the the 500-seat lower house, so any group aspiring to form a government must keep its options open -- and its policies noncommital -- in the hunt for future coalition partners.

One thing about Japanese politics remains unchanged after years of musical-chair governments by parties who've changed their policy stances, leaders and names -- campaigns are not about issues or policies, they are about surviving elections.

While the LDP fans election fever, its coalition partners the Social Democratic Party and New Party Sakigake are decidely cool toward early elections under a revised polling system predicted to be unkind to smaller groups like theirs.

Lower house elections, which are not mandated until next July, will be held under a first-past-the-post system introduced to replace a unique multi-seat system, which in some districts allowed even fifth-place finishers to gain office with the backing of narrow interest groups.
Replacing the cozy old system with a more competitive one was supposed to turn elections from largely pork-barrel spending contests to clashes over the issues of the day.

"One theory was that the single-seat system would sharpen policy-oriented political debate and that there would be contentious issues that would divide the Japanese political world into two more or less equal camps," said LDP Secretary General Koichi Kato.

"The new electoral system is already having an effect on political debate," Kato told a news conference. "But I doubt many...keen observers of Japanese domestic politics would say that the effect has been one of sharpening debate."

Echoing observations of analysts and laments of voters -- who are projected to stay away from the coming elections in record numbers -- Kato says campaign debate has become "more vague rather than more focused".

"Everyone and every party says they're in favour of reforming and streamlining the bureaucracy," quipped Soichiro Tahara, a caustic television political commentator. "But ask about specifics and the conversation goes nowhere."
Policy issues are conspicuously absent from the hectares of newsprint major dailies have devoted to politics since the electoral race began heating up last month.

Instead, readers who braved the political pages saw blow-by-blow accounts of the struggle over an election date -- October 20 versus October 27 -- and the squabbles among a band of young reformists over whom to invite or exclude from a new party they are forming.
